comments.value:
1st: that wouldnt change a thing and encourage people to mod the SDK (like people did in the early days to remove the 20k poly limit)
2nd: vrchats "Performance rating" does not cover some optimization steps and is more a guideline.
Example for the 2nd point:
69.999 poly avatar: good
70.001 poly avatar: very poor
That one is probably the one that makes the less sense to have such a hard transition from good to very poor. Also their system does not take blendshapes into account. (Idk if they can code that tbh, Im not a unity developer) But one optimization process is isolating blendshapes into an own mesh to reduce the amount of blendshape calculation. That increases potential material and mesh counts, meaning leaning you more to the "very poor" rating while you are actually doing a good thing performance wise.

@{5f2def4d22470972dc58f6a2|full_name}: Hadn't seen this reply until now sorry, my point is more to guilt trip users into following the rules. If you mod the SDK to remove the message, you clearly know you're doing something and have to accept that fact. If every time you upload you see a warning about your avatar's performance, there's a 'good chance' you need to optimize. Obviously users can have many gesture-linked objects to activate and this can make you 'Very Poor' even if none are active, but at that point you know the cause of the issue and can ignore the message right?
The point is mainly to bring attention to avatar performance as right now MANY people completely ignore avatar performance and simply blame the game as a whole, even though their avatar has more materials and polygons than some entire games.
"Why optimize if it lets me upload anyway?" is the mentality the majority of users have unfortunately!

@{5ae5c147906bfd12e600dc47|full_name}: I see your point, but with your suggestion you still punish literally everyone who tries to optimize as good as possible and still lands in the very poor state into wasting 5-10 secs every upload just to click the message away. During testing it happens very quickly that you upload an avi 20-30 times, with a 10 second cooldown you would force someone into in that case to wait for roughly 5 minutes - wasting time and in perspective of someone who creates and sells avatars - money.

@{5f2def4d22470972dc58f6a2|full_name}: I think that's more a problem with VRChat's ranking than a problem with this idea though!
It ranks based on what the worse possible performance 'could' be, say all meshes are active for example. Obviously most avatars just toggle on say a sword or something and toggle it off again.
However... Some others have entire layers of clothing instead of using individual avatars for that, so they can have maybe 6 to 8 different skinned meshes active at once, which is pretty horrible for performance!

@{5ae5c147906bfd12e600dc47|full_name}: i dont see the issue with having 6 to 8 layers active? I do that myself on my most used avatar, 6 renderers, 230k tris, 23 mats and all feedback i gain to this avatar is "unusual good performance", despite it having 14 independent toggleable clothing pieces. Everything in this game regarding user content is how the people create it. You say "6 to 8 layers is horrible" - i say "6 to 8 layers is nothing if you know what you are doing".
However, that you want to make people aware of bad performing avatars is what you are after and thats completly legit, but you always have to keep in mind that what you are currently suggesting is also hurting people which are doing decently.

@{5f2def4d22470972dc58f6a2|full_name}: Your avatar is quite literally a performance nightmare. It's worth noting how Unity renders, you can actually test in the scene to see how many draw calls your avatar is. :)
Basically every mesh is rendered as its own object, and every material on that mesh is its own draw call. There's no instancing at work with avatars really.
My avatar is 1 skinned mesh, 2 materials, 69,000 tris. It looks perfectly fine, if I need different clothes I just switch avatar. I have a Quest version uploaded too at 19,000 tris.
The bigger performance issue if you have a good GPU is Dynamic Bones really, especially for those with Ryzen 7/9 or Core i9 CPUs. High-end CPUs really struggle on the single-core front. (Hopefully 'Avatar physics' helps address this!)
For some perspective, your avatar is more polys than some entire games. :)
Avatar picture attached to show that you can make a perfectly fine looking avatar within VRChat's recommendations:

@{5ae5c147906bfd12e600dc47|full_name}: "literally a performance nightmare" you are welcome to join me any time and try it out if my avatar brings you to lag - i would be very surprised if it would. I know a lot of "1 mesh, 150k, 20mat" avatars that perform way worse than mine. 
Anyway, I know that one *can* do good looking avatars within spec (since one of mine is that as well, but she is purely for >70 ppl lobbies) but keep in mind that in some circumstances it simply does not fit within the current ranking of vrchats system. 
That the most seen issue with performance is the single core load (especially with a lot of dynamic bones and higher amount of draw calls) is out of the question, after that comes avatars with blendshapes on "highish" skinned mesh renderers, which cause unnecessary gpu blendshape calculations on the mesh. (That includes your 1 mesh 69k poly as well, as stated in the docs if your face has visemes ;) )
But that brings us back to where your initial idea started. Where to begin reminding people that something is not done well and how to remind them properly, without interfering with the ones who are doing their best and due to limitations dont reach a better rating? (In my "horrible" avatar case its the least amount of materials i am able to use due to shader limitations, otherwise i would atlas even more) (Please keep in mind that avatar 3.0 features at some point tempt to making more materials, bones or meshes being used) Cause once you interfere too much, modded SDKs will probably rise again and thats something one should try to avoid in my opinion.
PS: 24 drawcalls and i know that - if worlds use real time light with shadow calculations we would come to the point of world opimization.

@{5f2def4d22470972dc58f6a2|full_name}: Yeahhhh, this is the issue really! There's a fine line between not interfering too much, and not doing anything to encourage optimization.
I'm sure you've seen the attitude people have too, the whole "I don't know how to optimize" or "Optimizing an avatar makes it look bad", etc. - There's nothing encouraging people to optimize avatars, they simply say "VRChat performs bad, bad devs" and conclude that's the reason for poor performance versus user content. :)
VRChat is by no means extremely optimized right now, but user content obliterates what little usage the VRChat core uses. There needs to be 'something' to encourage optimization without enforcing hard limits like other games do.

This does not make sense as long as the system does not consider toggles and 3.0.
And even if that whole system got reworked I think it is better to choose what to see in the client rather than pester the uploader.

details:
Add a warning message when uploading a 'Very Poor' avatar mentioning that this avatar may lower other user's framerate, advise the user optimize.

Maybe have a cooldown of 5 or 10 seconds before this message can be closed to encourage users to take it seriously?
(The WinRAR 'evaluation edition' strategy!)

Edit: Clarifying that I don't mean block uploading, I mean make the user wait 5 or 10 seconds before they can continue to upload, simply to remind the user to try optimizing the avatar. Make them feel bad for now doing it.
title: Add warning message when uploading 'Very Poor' avatar
